title: Publications
text:
Anna E. Murphy, Ashley N. Bulseco, Ross Ackerman, Joseph H. Vineis, and Jennifer L. Bowen. (2020). Sulphide addition favours respiratory ammonification (DNRA) over complete denitrification and alters the active microbial community in salt marsh sediments. Environmental Microbiology, 22(6), 2124-2139. DOI HTML


Abstract

Summary The balance between nitrate respiration pathways, denitrification and dissimilatory nitrate (NO3−) reduction to ammonium (DNRA), determines whether bioavailable nitrogen is removed as N2 gas or recycled as ammonium. Saltwater intrusion and organic matter enrichment may increase sulphate reduction leading to sulphide accumulation. We investigated the effects of sulphide on the partitioning of NO3− between complete denitrification and DNRA and the microbial communities in salt marsh sediments. Complete denitrification significantly decreased with increasing sulphide, resulting in an increase in the contribution of DNRA to NO3− respiration. Alternative fates of NO3− became increasingly important at higher sulphide treatments, which could include N2O production and/or transport into intracellular vacuoles. Higher 16S transcript diversity was observed in the high sulphide treatment, with clear shifts in composition. Generally, low and no sulphide, coupled with high NO3−, favoured the activity of Campylobacterales, Oceanospirillales and Altermonadales, all of which include opportunistic denitrifiers. High ∑sulphide conditions promoted the activity of potential sulphide oxidizing nitrate reducers (Desulfobulbaceae, Acidiferrobacteraceae and Xanthomonadales) and sulphate reducers (Desulfomonadaceae, Desulfobacteraceae). Our study highlights the tight coupling between N and S cycling, and the implications of these dynamics on the fate of bioavailable N in coastal environments susceptible to intermittent saltwater inundation and organic matter enrichment.

title: Ashley Bulseco
text:
Bio
Ashley’s research focuses on understanding the microbial response to human-driven disturbances in wetland, estuarine, and marine ecosystems. She is particularly interested in whether shifts in the microbial community translate to changes in ecosystem function, especially in relation to carbon and nitrogen cycling. Ashley’s work often takes a multi-faceted approach to address these questions, applying a range of interdisciplinary techniques that combine field work, controlled laboratory experiments, biogeochemical measurements, sequencing, and bioinformatics. Prior to coming to UNH, she taught Environmental Science and Oceanography at the high school level and will continue to explore her passion for innovative and inclusive pedagogical practices in STEM.

title: Erin Mansfield
text:
Bio
Erin’s is a Master’s student whose research focuses on the salt marsh restoration strategy of thin layer placement in the Wells National Estuarine Research Reserve in Maine. She is interested in understanding how microbial communities and the biogeochemical cycles they mediate respond over time after restoration, with the long-term goal of understanding how incorporating microbial monitoring may provide a deeper understanding of restoration success. She is also assisting a project focused on characterizing oyster microbiomes in Great Bay, NH. During her graduate studies and in her future career, she hopes to connect with local communities and stakeholders for collaboration and to share her research.

title: Hannah Holland-Moritz
text:
Bio
Hannah Holland-Moritz is a consulting bioinformatics specialist in the Bulseco group. She also maintains a research program at Syracuse University where she is a Research Assistant Professor. Her research focuses on integrating microbial traits and eco-evolutionary dynamics into predictive models at the community, landscape, and global scales. By combining microbial community data, molecular tools, and quantitative modeling, she examines how microbial traits and interactions mediate carbon and nutrient cycling in terrestrial and synthetic ecosystems. Her research addresses a wide-range of challenges from predicting which bacteria in fermented foods produce flavor-enhancing metabolites to identifying the microorganisms most likely to contribute to climate change in wetlands and polar regions. In addition to her research, Holland-Moritz is an active and enthusiastic supporter of the science of team science and enjoys training and mentoring students in interdisciplinary leadership, informatics, and data science skills.

Thanks for visiting this webpage, it’s still under construction, if you want to know more about the lab, please reach out to Ashley Bulseco directly.
A longstanding objective in microbial ecology is to link spatial and temporal distributions of microorganisms to ecosystem function and global biogeochemical cycling. As a microbial and ecosystem ecologist, I apply a combination of controlled laboratory experiments and field-based studies that employ next-generation sequencing, bioinformatics, and biogeochemical rate measurements, ultimately aiming to connect biological mechanisms to ecosystem scale processes using a microbial lens. Primary research goals including understanding changes to microbial diversity, structure, and function of coastal ecosystems in response to human activities, and in turn, using microbiome-informed data as an indication of overall ecosystem health. My research program is designed for extensive intellectual contribution and involvement from both undergraduate and graduate students. If you are interested in joining the lab, please reach out!
Learn about our research

title: Marley Gonsalves
text:
Bio
Marley is a PhD student whose research focuses on phytoplankton and bacterial community networks in estuarine and saltmarsh systems. She is interested in understanding how phytoplankton community composition changes in concert with other microbes, and how those changes relate to carbon cycling and other ecosystem functions. Marley is co-advised by Dr. Elizabeth Harvey, and her work focuses on combining molecular techniques and bioinformatics with traditional and imaging flow cytometry. Her current projects include: - tracking microbial community composition in coastal New Hampshire via a multu-year time series - characterizing microbial communities in salt marsh pools - assessing impacts of restoration on microbial carbon cycling in salt marsh pools Science communication Instagram: @mgg_plankton

title: Camille Kroot
text:
Bio
Camille is a master’s student at the University of New Hampshire. Her thesis project investigates microbial community composition and nitrogen cycling in restored New Hampshire salt marshes, particularly if there are noticeable shifts in community and ecosystem function when comparing restored marshes to degraded and healthy marshes. She has participated and led a variety of field work, incubations, and lab work to gain a deeper understanding of microbial communities in changing environments, and their implications. In the future, Camille hopes to pursue a career that combines research and collaboration with the public to connect people to science.

title: Seren Davies
text:
Bio
Seren Davies is a sophomore genetics major at the University of New Hampshire. Originally from Bristol, Rhode Island, she has worked with Dr. Ashley Bulseco’s MicroEco lab for over a year. During this time, she has pursued research regarding the microbial communities within salt marshes and the ways these are altered by the changing environment. In addition, she serves as a student ambassador for the Hamel Center for Undergraduate Research, an executive member for UNH’s Alpha Phi Omega, an employee of the Audubon Society of Rhode Island, and a member of the UNH Honors College.
